text: Be honest about what you do not know. Flag every uncertainty and tell me how confident you really are.
Do not pretend to certainty you lack. Where the evidence is thin or you are guessing, say so plainly and hedge appropriately.
Calibrate your confidence carefully. Distinguish what you are sure of from what is merely plausible, and mark the shaky parts.
Acknowledge the limits of your knowledge. Point out what could change the answer and where you might be wrong.
Tell me your uncertainty out loud: attach a rough confidence level to each claim and note anything you cannot verify.
Stay epistemically humble. Avoid overclaiming, admit the gaps in your reasoning, and be upfront when something is unknown.
Where you are unsure, do not paper over it. Name the ambiguity, give ranges instead of false precision, and own the doubt.
Be candid about your confidence. Separate the solid parts of your answer from the speculative ones and label each.
If you are not sure, say so. I would rather have an honest it-depends than a confident guess dressed up as fact.
Report how much you actually know. Mark the claims you can back up and the ones that are only educated guesses.
Do not overstate. Where the answer is genuinely uncertain, tell me the odds and what would resolve the doubt.
Be transparent about the unknowns. Highlight what is missing, what you are assuming, and how that limits your answer.
Give me a calibrated response: confidence for the parts you trust, explicit caution for the parts you do not.
Admit uncertainty rather than hiding it. Flag anything provisional and explain why it might not hold.
Be upfront about doubt. If the evidence is weak or conflicting, tell me so instead of forcing a firm answer.
Say clearly how confident you are in each part, and single out the claims most likely to be wrong.
